```{r include=FALSE}
library(fracdiff)
library(astsa)
data(varve,package = "astsa")
```


## Long Memory ARMA
The ARMA process can be written as a linear process $x_t=\sum\limits_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j w_{t-j}$ and it can be shown that coefficients in the representation dominated by exponential decay. For example the ARMA(1,1) under the linear representations becomes

\begin{align*}
&x_t = \phi x_{t-1}+w_t+\theta w_{t-1}\\
\implies &x_t - \phi x_{t-1} = w_t+\theta w_{t-1}\\
\implies &(1 - \phi B)x_{t} = (1+\theta B)w_{t}\\
\implies &x_{t} = (1+\theta B) \frac{1}{1 - \phi B}w_{t}\\
&\quad = (1+\theta B) \sum_{i=0}^\infty (\phi B)^i w_{t}\\
&\quad = \left[\sum_{i=0}^\infty (\phi B)^i + \sum_{i=0}^\infty (\phi B)^i (\theta B)\right] w_{t}\\
&\quad = [1 + (\phi B) + (\phi B)^2 + (\phi B)^3 + (\phi B)^4 + \dots\\
&\qquad~\qquad (\theta B) + (\theta B)(\phi B) + (\theta B)(\phi B)^2 + (\theta B)(\phi B)^3+\dots]\\
&\quad = [1 + (\phi B) + (\phi B)^2 + (\phi B)^3 + (\phi B)^4 + \dots\\
&\qquad~\qquad (\theta B) + (\theta )(\phi B^2) + (\theta )(\phi^2B^3) + (\theta )(\phi^3 B^4)+\dots]\\
&= [1 + (\phi+\theta )B + (\phi^2 + (\theta )\phi )B^2 + (\phi ^2+(\theta )\phi ^2)B^3 +\\
&~\quad (\phi^4+(\theta )\phi^3)B^4 + \dots]w_t\\
&= [1 + (\phi + \theta )B + \phi(\phi + \theta )B^2 + \phi^2(\phi + \theta )B^3 + \phi^3(\phi + \theta )B^4 + \dots]w_t\\
&= w_t + (\phi + \theta )w_{t-1} + \phi(\phi + \theta )w_{t-2} + \phi^2(\phi + \theta )w_{t-3} + \phi ^3(\phi + \theta )w_{t-4} + \dots\\
\end{align*}

So here we can see the effect of the past is quickly fading as there is exponential terms. This result implies the ACF of the short memory process satisfies $\rho(h)\to0$ exponentially fast as $h \to\infty$. When the sample ACF of a time series decays slowly the advice given to difference the series until it seems stationary.

This process has a drawback which is we can only choose the discrete difference values as {0,1,2,...} which may sometime leads to under or over differencing of the original process. The long memory ARMA is intermediate compromises between $\text{ARIMA}(p,d = 0,q)$ and $\text{ARIMA}(p,d = 1,q)$ models.

## ARFIMA(0,d,0) Model

Instead of the fully integrated model we are addressing it with fractional component which make the abbreviation as Auto Regression Fractional Integrated Moving Average model. The basic ARFIMA(1,d,1) model becomes

\begin{align*}
&\Phi(B)(1-B)^bx_t = \Theta(B)w_t\qquad |b|\in [0,.5)\quad \Phi(B)=\Theta(B)=1\\
\implies&(1-B)^bx_t = w_t\\
\implies&x_t= (1-B)^{-b}w_t\\
&\quad= \sum_{j = 0}^\infty \frac{\Gamma(j+d)}{\Gamma(j+1)\Gamma(d)} w_{t-j}\\
&\quad= \sum_{j = 0}^\infty \psi_j w_{t-j}\\
Cov(x_t,x_{t+h}) &= Cov\left(\sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_jw_{t-j}, \sum_{k=0}^\infty \psi_kw_{t+h-k}\right)\\
&= Cov\left(\sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_jw_{t-j}, \sum_{j+h=0}^\infty \psi_{j+h}w_{t+h-(j+h)}\right) \quad [t-j=t+h-k\implies k=j+h]\\
&= Cov\left(\sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j w_{t-j}, \sum_{j=-h}^\infty \psi_{j+h}w_{t-j}\right)\\
&=\sigma_w^2 \sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_j \psi_{j+h}\\
&=\sigma_w^2 \sum \frac{\Gamma(j+d)}{\Gamma(j+1)\Gamma(d)}\times \frac{\Gamma(j+h+d)}{\Gamma(j+h+1)\Gamma(d)}\\
\gamma(h)&=\sigma_w^2 \frac{\Gamma(1-2d)}{\Gamma(1-d)^2}\frac{\Gamma(h+d)}{\Gamma(h+1-d)}\\
\gamma(0)&=\sigma_w^2 \frac{\Gamma(1-2d)}{\Gamma(1-d)^2}\frac{\Gamma(d)}{\Gamma(1-d)}\\
\rho(h)&=\frac{\gamma(h)}{\gamma(0)}= \frac{\Gamma(h+d)\Gamma(1-d)}{\Gamma(h+1-d)\Gamma(d)} \approx h^{2d-1} \quad \text{For large }h\\
&\sum_{h=-\infty}^{+\infty} |h^{2d-1}| = \infty \qquad |h|\in [0,0.5)
\end{align*}

Here this is known as the long memory as the ACF series converges to finite values.

## Parameter Estimation ARFIMA(0,d,0)

The parameter estimation process involves minimizing the sum of squares $Q(d)=\sum w_t^2(d)$. Here, one notable thing is that the long memory ARIMA can model data without the help of any other AR or MA parameters. The only parameter $d$ can be used to describe the long memory process.

\begin{align*}
w_t(d) &= \sum (1-B)^d x_t\\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \frac{\Gamma(j-d)}{\Gamma(j+1)\Gamma(-d)} x_t\\
&= \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \pi_j(d) x_t\qquad \pi_0(d)=1\\
Q(d)&=\sum w_t^2(d)\\
Q'(d)&= 2\sum_{t=1}^n w_t(d) w_t'(d)\\
Q''(d)&= 2\sum_{t=1}^n [w_t'(d)^2+ w_t(d)w_t''(d)]\approx 2\sum_{t=1}^n w_t'(d)^2\\
d_{(k+1)} &= d_{(k)} - \frac{Q'(d)}{Q''(d)}\\
&= d_{(k)} - \frac{\sum_{t=1}^n w_t(d) w_t'(d)}{\sum_{t=1}^n w_t'(d)^2}\\
\end{align*}

## Model fitting

Here we are fitting the ARIMA(1,1,1) and the ARFIMA(0,d,0) model to the log-verbe data. The plot below shows the ACF of the residuals for both of the models. As all the ACF values are with in the two dashed line so there is no evidence of correlation between the residuals. So both of the model fits the data well. We omitted the first 30 observations $w_i$ for the computaion to take care of the long memory bevavior.


```{r fig.height=7}
library(fracdiff)
data(varve,package = "astsa")
lvarve = log(varve) - mean(log(varve))
varve.fd = fracdiff(lvarve, nar = 0, nma = 0, M = 30)


res.fd = diffseries(log(varve), varve.fd$d)
res.arima = resid(arima(log(varve), order = c(1, 1, 1)))
par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
acf(res.arima, 100, xlim = c(4, 97), ylim = c(-.2, .2), main = "ACF for the residuals of ARIMA(1,1,1)")
acf(res.fd, 100, xlim = c(4, 97), ylim = c(-.2, .2), main = "ACF for the residuals of ARIMA(0,0.384,0)")
```


## Forcasting

The one step ahead prediction can be obtained by considering converting the ARFIMA model to the linear process. $m$ step ahead prediction can be obtained sequantially.

\begin{align*}
&\sum_{j=0}^\infty \pi_j(d) x_{t-j} = w_t\\
\implies& x_{t}+\sum_{j=1}^\infty \pi_j(d) x_{t-j} = w_t\qquad\pi_0(d)=1\\
\implies& x_{t} = w_t-\sum_{j=1}^\infty \pi_j(d) x_{t-j}\\
\implies& \hat{x}_{t} = -\sum_{j=1}^{n-1} \pi_j(\hat{d}) x_{t-j}\\
\implies& \tilde{x}_{n+m}^n = -\sum_{j=1}^{n} \pi_j(\hat{d}) \tilde{x}_{n+m-j}^n\\
\end{align*}

## ARFIMA(p,d,q) Model

The full model can be written as 
$$
\phi(B)\nabla^d(x_t-\mu)=\theta(B)w_t
$$

Where $|d|\in [0,.5)$ and the positive values indicate persistancy and the negative values indicates lack of persistance. For estimating the parameter we need the equation 
$$
w_t=\sum_{j=0}^\infty \pi_j(x_{t-j}-\mu)
$$

And for forcasting we are going to need the equation
$$
x_t=\mu+\sum_{j=0}^\infty \psi_jw_{t-j}
$$

## Frequency Domain Approach

The frequency $\omega$ in the frequency domain approach can be estimated using the equation below where we are skipping the intermediate details steps and derrivations
$$
f_x(\omega) = \frac{\sigma_w^2}{|\sum_{k=0}^\infty \pi_ke^{-2\pi ik\omega}|^2}=[4sin^2(\pi\omega)]^{-d}\sigma_w^2
$$

## Parameter Estimation (Frequency Domain Approach)

The likelihood based method is used to estinate the parameter value form the spectram analysis
\begin{align*}
f_x(\omega_k; d, \sigma_w^2) &= \sigma_w^2\, g_k^{-d};\qquad g_k = 4 \sin^2(\pi \omega_k)\\
\ln L(x; d, \sigma_w^2)&\approx -m \ln \sigma_w^2 + d \sum_{k=1}^{m} \ln g_k-\frac{1}{\sigma_w^2} \sum_{k=1}^{m} g_k^{\,d} I(\omega_k)\qquad m=n/2-1\\
\hat{\sigma}_w^2(d)&= \frac{1}{m} \sum_{k=1}^{m} g_k^{\,d} I(\omega_k)\\
\end{align*}

```{r eval=FALSE}
series = log(varve) # specify series to be analyzed
d0 <-  .1 # initial value of d

n.per = nextn(length(series))
m = (n.per)/2 - 1
per = Mod(fft(series-mean(series))[-1])^2 # remove 0 freq and
per = per/n.per # scale the peridogram
g = 4*(sin(pi*((1:m)/n.per))^2)
# Function to calculate -log.likelihood
whit.like = function(d){
  g.d <- g^d
  sig2 <- (sum(g.d*per[1:m])/m)
  log.like <- m*log(sig2) - d*sum(log(g)) + m
  return(log.like) 
  }

est = optim(d0, whit.like, gr=NULL, method="L-BFGS-B", hessian=TRUE,lower=-.5, upper=.5, control=list(trace=1,REPORT=1))
```

```{r include=FALSE}
series = log(varve) # specify series to be analyzed
d0 <-  .1 # initial value of d

n.per = nextn(length(series))
m = (n.per)/2 - 1
per = Mod(fft(series-mean(series))[-1])^2 # remove 0 freq and
per = per/n.per # scale the peridogram
g = 4*(sin(pi*((1:m)/n.per))^2)
# Function to calculate -log.likelihood
whit.like = function(d){
  g.d <- g^d
  sig2 <- (sum(g.d*per[1:m])/m)
  log.like <- m*log(sig2) - d*sum(log(g)) + m
  return(log.like) 
  }

est = optim(d0, whit.like, gr=NULL, method="L-BFGS-B", hessian=TRUE,lower=-.5, upper=.5, control=list(trace=1,REPORT=1))
```


```{r}
cat("d.hat =", est$par,"se(dhat) =",1/sqrt(est$hessian),"\n")
```


```{r}
cat("d.hat =", varve.fd$d,"se(dhat) =",varve.fd$stderror.dpq,"\n")
```
